html:
The Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata was the last and shortest-lived of Spain's viceroyalties in the Americas, created in 1776 with its capital at Buenos Aires. It covered roughly today's Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia.

Spain carved it out of the Viceroyalty of Peru to block Portuguese Brazil and British smugglers in the River Plate. It included Upper Peru, so the silver of Potosí now flowed out through Buenos Aires instead of Lima. Free trade within the empire, allowed from 1778, made Buenos Aires grow fast on silver, hides and beef.

In 1806 and 1807 British forces captured Buenos Aires and then Montevideo. Local militias, not Spanish troops, drove them out, and the people of Buenos Aires learned their own strength. When Napoleon overthrew the Spanish king, the city's leaders set up their own government in the May Revolution of 1810. The viceroyalty broke apart in the independence wars, into the United Provinces, Paraguay, Uruguay and Bolivia.
